title: Article X · Whether the philosophical knowledge of divine things deserves to be called contemplation

blocks.s: The Catholic doctors assign this difference between theological and philosophical wisdom: that theological wisdom is affective or formed by divine love, for which reason it is truly and properly called wisdom — that is, a savoury knowledge. Hence it is also asserted to be unitive, since through the affection of charity it joins the created mind to God. Hence also its act is properly called contemplation. But philosophical wisdom is only speculative, formless and bare: therefore, according to Hugh on the Angelic Hierarchy, it was not for life, and was to be found and administered by those who were not sons of life, namely the philosophers — of whom the Apostle says that although they had known God, they did not glorify him as God but vanished in their thoughts (Rom. i, 21).

It must be answered that the philosophers who knew only the natural happiness of the soul spoke also of natural love of God alone, and of those virtues which can be obtained by natural virtue and human study. But these do not suffice for salvation. Therefore in them there was no sincere knowledge of divine things; and they erred in many ways, though they said some things true and subtle. Their speculation therefore does not properly and completely deserve the name of contemplation. Nor were they truly perfect, but only according to their own opinion, by which they placed the highest perfection in the natural virtues. For their knowledge was not anointed with the affection of that charity which alone makes the mind pleasing to God — namely divine, supernatural, infused charity, by which the knowledge of divine things that is called contemplation must be formed and perfected.
